You are analyzing an SF1000 TPC-H profiling campaign of StarRocks-on-Sirius (a GPU SQL engine embedded in a StarRocks compute node, "CN").
Read /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/WORKFLOW-PLAN.md first: it lists every evidence file, the tools and the facts already established. Evidence root: /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000. Source tree: /home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/perf
(engine C++ under src/, CN Rust under experimental/starrocks/src, translator under experimental/starrocks/crates/starrocks-plan-translator, StarRocks FE Java under experimental/starrocks/starrocks/fe).
Key pre-digested files: /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/results.md (timings per arm), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/survey/plan-summary.txt and /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/survey/explain/qNN.costs.txt (FE plans), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/card-compare-cn1.txt and card-compare-cn4.txt (FE estimate vs actual rows per exchange),
/tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1-cnlog.txt / cn4-cnlog.txt (+ .json: per run fragments, declared cardinalities, nixl transmits, OOM reschedules), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1-quent.txt / cn4-quent.txt / standalone-quent.txt (+ .json: task state time, reservation vs peak, batches, dwell, staging leases),
/tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1-ops.txt etc (per-operator Computing time), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/standalone/runs/qNN.explain.txt (DuckDB/Sirius plan of the same SQL), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/cn1/dump/ (FE fragment params + Substrait per fragment), /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/compare-*.txt (oracle correctness).
You may run the python tools in /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000 and read the source; do not modify the source tree, do not start clusters or GPU jobs (they are exclusive resources owned by the orchestrator), do not write outside /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/agent-notes/.
The three focus dimensions are: (A) query planning, (B) cardinality estimation, (C) backpressure (memory pressure, parked intermediates, staging leases, queue waits, OOM reschedules, scaling 1->4 CN).
Every finding must cite concrete evidence (file + the line or number) and, where it proposes a change, name the file/function and rate confidence. Distinguish measured facts from inference.

Your family: multi-fragment-small. Queries: q02 q11 q15. Focus: many small fragments, GATHER/SHUFFLE hops, per-fragment fixed overhead, and the q15 run-to-run row-count difference (streams 18/22 carried 0 rows in one run: relate to float-sum determinism and the SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS gate; check the canon vs nocanon follow-up arms if present).
Work through the evidence for these queries in all arms (cn1, cn4, standalone, plus standalone-failed / q15 canon arms if present), read the relevant source when a mechanism matters (engine.rs run_fragment_inner, local_exchange.rs, gpu_pipeline_executor.cpp reschedule loop, exchange_staging_arena.cpp, the FE StatisticsCalculator and the join distribution rules), and produce 3-8 findings ranked by impact. Prefer fewer, well-evidenced findings. Write your working notes to /tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad/perf/sf1000/agent-notes/multi-fragment-small.md (tables you computed, commands you ran) and return the findings as structured output.

- ooc-sort-dev: Use when developing, building, testing, or iterating on the disk-backed (out-of-core) sort implementation for cudf-polars in ~/bzaitlen/test-data/ooc-sort/. Covers installing into the rapidsmpf container env, running streaming sort tests, and the phase-by-phase implementation workflow.
- build-errors: Use this skill when the build fails, compilation errors occur, or you see undefined references, linker errors, CUDA compilation issues, missing headers, or template instantiation failures. Analyzes errors, suggests fixes, and iteratively rebuilds until success.
- build-sirius-starrocks: Build the Sirius-as-StarRocks-CN stack on a fresh GPU box — UCX, nixl, libsirius, StarRocks FE, and the Rust CN. Use when standing the stack up from scratch, recovering a broken toolchain (g++/ld/nvml shims, CUDA 13, no-root conda deps), applying the StarRocks proto patch, or relocating pixi/cargo/Maven onto local NVMe.
- cn-tuning: Size Sirius StarRocks CN memory and operator budgets for a given GPU box and TPC-H scale factor. Use when choosing GPU_MEM, STAGING, HOST_MEM, hash_partition_bytes, scan_task_batch_size, or when a query OOMs / exhausts the exchange arena / looks like an engine bug that is actually mis-sizing. Covers the derived-flag path vs a full sirius.yaml.
- dataset-manager: Use this skill to generate benchmark datasets (TPC-H, TPC-DS, etc.). Trigger when the user needs test data at a specific scale factor for benchmarking or testing. Supports parquet and duckdb output formats.
- log-analyzer: Use this skill to analyze Sirius query execution logs — to find why a query is slow, diagnose validation errors (wrong results), spot excessive downgrading, identify pipeline gaps, or compare two runs of the same query. Trigger whenever the user mentions a Sirius log file, says "look at this log", asks about per-operator time, pipeline gaps, memory pressure, downgrade behavior, validation/correctness mismatches, or wants to compare two query runs. Also use as a hand-off target from race-check (for two-run comparisons), runtime-errors (for "where did the query stall before hang"), and validate (for diffing the bad run against a good run). This is the log-only counterpart to profile-analyzer (nsys) and optimization-advisor (source-level guidance).
- module-context: Automatically identify which dependency library modules are relevant to a task and load their API documentation into context. Use PROACTIVELY before implementing features, fixing bugs, or writing new operators — analyzes the task description and loads cudf, rmm, duckdb, cucascade module docs to improve code quality. Trigger when the user asks to implement, add, fix, or modify GPU operators, pipeline components, memory management, joins, aggregations, sorting, expressions, or data I/O.
- module-discover: Discover and document a dependency library or submodule — analyzes all uses within the codebase, divides the library into logical modules, identifies which modules are used, and generates LLM-consumable API documentation for each module. Use when the user wants to understand a library dependency, map its modules, or generate API reference docs for a submodule.
- optimization-advisor: Use this skill to find exactly which source code to optimize for better GPU performance. Maps nsys profile hotspots to specific Sirius source files and functions, classifies bottlenecks as GPU-bound, CPU-bound, or sync-bound, and recommends actionable code changes. Trigger when the user wants to know what to optimize, where to focus coding effort, or wants source-level optimization guidance. This skill focuses on actionable source code targets — for generating performance reports and measurements, use profile-analyzer instead.
- pr-digest: Generates a "learning" PR-review digest — a markdown file at PR_digests/PR_digest_<N>.md that explains what a GitHub PR does, why, and exactly where in the code, with clickable file/line links and trimmed diffs. Use this whenever the user shares a GitHub PR URL (e.g. github.com/owner/repo/pull/1234) and wants to understand, summarize, review, walk through, or get up to speed on what changed — phrases like "can you review this PR", "what does this PR do", "help me understand this pull request", "summarize the changes in PR
- pre-commit-cleanup: Clean the current Git changes before committing. Use when preparing to commit or when the pre-commit cleanliness hook blocks a commit.
- profile-analyzer: Use this skill to understand why a Sirius query is slow, identify GPU bottlenecks, or detect performance regressions. Generates reports with kernel occupancy, memory bandwidth, operator attribution, and cross-run comparisons. Trigger when the user mentions profiling, nsys, GPU utilization, kernel analysis, performance reports, or wants to compare query timings across runs. This skill focuses on measurement and reporting — for mapping hotspots to source code fixes, use optimization-advisor instead.
- skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- tpch-2host: Bring up Sirius StarRocks CNs across two physical GB200 hosts with nixl over cross-host NVLink, and the matching stock StarRocks (engine B) two-machine baseline. Use when replicating the two-host experiment, setting SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_ARENA=fabric, debugging a 0.4 GB/s cuda_ipc fallback, or running engine B as 1 FE + 1 BE per host.
- tpch-bench: Operate the Sirius-as-StarRocks-CN demo and its TPC-H benchmark on the 4x GB200 box. Use when bringing the multi-GPU (N-CN, one CN per GPU) cluster up or down, running a query or the 22-query sweep, verifying the nixl/NVLink transport, triaging a failing/hanging/slow query, checking results against DuckDB, or reproducing the A-vs-B comparison against stock StarRocks.
- tpch-cn-sweep: Run the 22-query TPC-H sweep against a Sirius StarRocks CN cluster on any box, scale factor, data path, or GPU count. Use when launching bench.sh, sizing GPU_MEM/STAGING, checking results against the DuckDB oracle, or triaging pass/wedge/refused rows. Not the in-process Sirius-vs-DuckDB benchmark skill; not the GB200-hardcoded tpch-bench ops skill.
- update-docs: Use this skill to update Super Sirius documentation after code changes. Trigger when the user says "update docs", "refresh documentation", "sync docs with code changes", or after merging PRs that changed the Super Sirius codebase. Inspects merged PRs since the last update and patches affected doc files.

Trigger for:
- Explicit learning requests: teach, explain, ELI5, walk me through, quiz me, flashcards, "I'm rusty on"; definitions ("what is X")
- Terse concept names implying "help me understand this": "Galois theory," "transformers, from scratch"
- Confusion signals: "won't stick," "keep mixing these up," "not getting it"

When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

21	## Facts established before the analysis
22	1. FE StatisticsCalculator.computeFileScanNode sets outputRowCount = 1 for FILES() scans ("we don't know the real schema in file, just use the default Row Count now"); every column statistic UNKNOWN. Hence every plan node has cardinality 1 and the CBO picks BROADCAST for most joins (orders 1.5B rows broadcast in q07/q09/q10..., lineitem 3.79B rows as the build side of q04's LEFT SEMI JOIN, partsupp 800M in q02).
23	2. Engine stream ids == FE exchange node ids; the receiver declares the exact parked row count per stream before build() ("declared input stream cardinality"), so DuckDB plans the receiver fragment with exact input cardinalities, but only after every sender finished (receiver-first rendezvous, local_exchange.rs). Nothing streams across a fragment boundary: the whole intermediate is parked on the GPU.
24	3. Engine OOM handling: gpu_pipeline_executor.cpp reschedules a task on OOM up to MAX_RETRIES=100 with a 50 ms sleep, then fails the query ("exceeded maximum retry limit"). It does not wait for memory to be released and cannot spill parked batches. q05 and q08 died this way on 1 CN at SF1000 (GPU_SCAN OOM, 101 s and 168 s).
25	4. Reserving.requested_bytes / peak_estimate vs Computing.peak_allocated_bytes (Quent task FSM) measure the engine's own memory estimation; standalone SF10 q01 requested 20.8 GB for a 5.6 GB peak.
26	
27	## Analysis dimensions (workflow)
28	A. Planning: per query, FE fragment tree and join distribution vs the DuckDB/Sirius standalone plan; what a stats-aware FE would choose; where the translator/CN could override (e.g. swap build/probe, refuse broadcast above a row threshold, local re-planning of a broadcast join once the actual parked cardinality is known).
29	B. Cardinality: FE estimate vs actual rows per exchange (card_compare), engine reservation estimate vs peak (quent_bp), the receiver-first exact-cardinality mechanism and its cost.
30	C. Backpressure: parked bytes and dwell per fragment, staging lease held/in-transit time and max concurrency vs SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_BYTES, Reserving/Queued waits, OOM reschedule storms, nixl transmit lease_ms/write_ms, 1-CN vs 4-CN scaling per query, standalone vs CN.
31	Each per-query analysis is verified adversarially (two skeptics with different lenses); the synthesis ranks findings with the evidence lines and proposes changes with file paths and confidence.
32

36	6. q15 returned 0 rows in run 1 and 1 row in runs 0 and 2 on 1 CN: streams 18 and 22 (the revenue = max(revenue) join output) carried 0 rows in run 1 while every other stream was identical.
37	   The build has the canonical float-sum sort gated OFF (SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS unset), so the two independently computed FP64 sums can differ in the last bits. Follow-up arms cn1-canon-q15 / cn1-nocanon-q15 test this.
38	7. Engine executor pools default to pipeline num_threads: 4 (docs/super-sirius/configuration.md:91-94); Quent "Queued" time per fragment is the wait for one of those slots plus the memory reservation gate.
39	   1-CN q04: scan fragment 37 tasks, Queued sum 19.9 s vs Computing 4.7 s inside a 1.2 s wall; join fragment requested 253 GB of reservations for a 61 GB summed peak (4x over-estimate).
40	8. Translator comment (node_translator.rs ~1924-1931) already records that the FE reports cardinality 1 for every FILES() scan and that nothing bounds a join build side; "bounding it belongs to the executor".
41	9. FE plans with 4 CNs alive are in survey/explain4/ (plan-summary-4cn.txt); diff against plan-summary.txt shows whether node count changes any distribution decision.
42	10. Plan-node enum decode for the dumps (TPlanNodeType(N)): survey/TPlanNodeType.map.txt (4 HASH_JOIN, 6 AGGREGATION, 8 SORT, 9 EXCHANGE, 17 FILE_SCAN, 28 PROJECT, ...).
43	11. The engine's DuckDB optimizer runs on every fragment (sirius_ffi.cpp:135, with STATISTICS_PROPAGATION and a few rewrites disabled, :233-240); the declared stream cardinality feeds the TableFunction cardinality callback (stream_bind_catalog.hpp:44-46), so build/probe choice inside a fragment sees exact stream sizes, but FILES() scans inside the same fragment carry DuckDB's parquet estimate. The FE's fragment cut (what is broadcast/shuffled) is fixed before any of this.
44	12. The FE's plan DEPENDS on the number of alive CNs even with cardinality 1 everywhere: with 4 CNs most joins flip from BROADCAST to PARTITIONED (shuffle) and fragment counts rise (q02 13->16, q08 11->16, q09 9->12; q03 orders join BROADCAST->PARTITIONED; q04/q12/q14/q19 BROADCAST->PARTITIONED; q15 -> BUCKET_SHUFFLE). survey/plan-summary.txt (1 CN) vs survey/plan-summary-4cn.txt (4 CNs); card-compare-cn4.txt uses the 4-CN plans (q03 exch2 = 3.23B lineitem rows shuffled, q12 exch1 = 1.5B orders rows shuffled).

Session-wide per CN ~3700 leases, max 94 concurrent (arena = 16 GiB).

CN arms: q02 q04 q06 q12 q13 q14 q20 q22 MATCH; q01 q07 q19 differ by 9.6e-4 and q03 by 1.8e-3 in revenue sums (the known `1 - 0.07` FP64->DECIMAL(16,2) truncation from #1236's lowering, not a multi-CN defect); q10 differs with maxreldiff 12.3 over 48 cells of its 20 rows, most likely the same truncated revenue sums reordering the TOP-20 (verify by comparing the customer sets and the revenue column); q15 differs by 1.1e-3 on its single row and is also flaky in row count (see fact 6); q11 shows EMPTY because the query returns 0 rows at SF1000 on both engines (the bench kit does not scale q11's 0.0001 fraction by 1/SF), so it is not a defect but the compare cannot confirm it.

50	18. Follow-up arms (may still be running while you work; use them only if their files exist): standalone-failed/runs/runs.csv (standalone Sirius on q05 q08 q09 q17 q18 q21), cn1-canon-q15/runs/runs.csv (1 CN, SIRIUS_CANONICAL_FLOAT_SUMS=1, 6 runs of q15) vs cn1-nocanon-q15/runs/runs.csv (gate off).

WITH
customer AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/customer/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
lineitem AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/lineitem/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
nation AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/nation/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
orders AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/orders/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
part AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/part/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
partsupp AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/partsupp/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
region AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/region/*.parquet","format"="parquet")),
supplier AS (SELECT * FROM FILES("path"="file://__TPCH_DATA__/supplier/*.parquet","format"="parquet"))
,
revenue AS (
    SELECT
        l_suppkey AS supplier_no,
        sum(l_extendedprice * (1 - l_discount)) AS total_revenue
    FROM
        lineitem
    WHERE
        l_shipdate >= CAST('1996-01-01' AS date)
      AND l_shipdate < CAST('1996-04-01' AS date)
    GROUP BY
        supplier_no
)
SELECT
    s_suppkey,
    s_name,
    s_address,
    s_phone,
    total_revenue
FROM
    supplier,
    revenue
WHERE
    s_suppkey = supplier_no
    AND total_revenue = (
        SELECT
            max(total_revenue)
        FROM revenue)
ORDER BY
    s_suppkey;

            supplier,

            AND n_name = 'GERMANY')

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Quent-instrumented CN capture at SF1000. usage: capture-cn.sh <num_cns> <tag> <timeout_s> <runs_after_warmup> q01 q03 ...
# Cluster: 100GiB GPU pool, 16GiB staging, 160GiB host per CN (the perf plan's retime configuration), watchdog 300 s,
# Quent on with per-fragment labels, async sender dispatch on. Telemetry dirs are wiped before launch so the newest
# session per CN is this arm's; after a clean SIGTERM the sessions are copied to <out>/quent/cn<i>/.
SP=/tmp/claude-1002/-home-prestouser-aocsa-sirius/25f3e903-c551-4a98-b7fc-a6e0ed53ade6/scratchpad
WT=/home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/perf; SR=$WT/experimental/starrocks; DATA=/scratch/sirius/datasets/tpch_sf1000
N=$1; TAG=$2; TO=$3; RUNS=$4; shift 4
OUT=$SP/perf/sf1000/$TAG; mkdir -p $OUT/quent
source $SP/cluster-env.sh $WT
export NUM_CNS=$N GPU_MEM=100GiB HOST_MEM=160GiB STAGING=16GiB SIRIUS_EXCHANGE_STAGING_BYTES=16GiB SIRIUS_QUERY_WATCHDOG_SECS=300
export SIRIUS_CN_ENABLE_QUENT=1 SIRIUS_CN_ASYNC_SENDER_DISPATCH=1
[ "$N" = 1 ] && { export SIRIUS_CN_DUMP_FRAGMENTS=$OUT/dump; mkdir -p $OUT/dump; rm -f $OUT/dump/*; }
M="mysql --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9030 --user root --batch --connect-timeout=5"
echo "##### CAPTURE $TAG NUM_CNS=$N queries: $* $(date -u +%T)"
pgrep -f "$SR/target/release/sirius-starrocks-cn" >/dev/null && { echo "REFUSING: CNs from this worktree still running"; exit 2; }
rm -rf $SR/.cn*/telemetry/*
bash $SP/start-cluster.sh $WT $OUT/cluster.log
for i in $(seq 1 60); do n=$($M -e "SHOW COMPUTE NODES;" 2>/dev/null | awk -F'\t' 'NR==1{for(i=1;i<=NF;i++) if($i=="Alive") c=i; next} $c=="true"{n++} END{print n+0}'); [ "$n" = "$N" ] && break; sleep 3; done
echo "alive=$n after $((i*3))s"; nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,memory.used --format=csv,noheader | tr '\n' ' '; echo
bash $SP/perf/sf1000/run-queries.sh $TAG $DATA $OUT/runs $TO $RUNS "$@"

"""Backpressure / estimation view of Quent ndjson sessions.

Per query label (CN labels are '<query id>:<fragment instance id>'; the query id prefix groups fragments) it reports:

  Reserving requested/peak_estimate vs Computing peak_allocated (memory estimation accuracy),
  data batches: count, bytes, dwell (Stationary -> hop/Destructed), staging leases: count, bytes, held time, InTransit time,
  max concurrent leases, stream hops (relayed/pushed) and scan_split_read statistics.
Sessions from several CNs may be passed together; results are keyed by label and session."""

    for run, o in json.load(open(sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--runs') + 1])).items():

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Run bench-kit TPC-H queries against the FE on 9030 with a /* marker */ so the FE audit log ties QueryId to (query, run).
# usage: run-queries.sh <tag> <tpch_data> <out_dir> <timeout_s> <runs_after_warmup> q01 q02 ...
# writes <out_dir>/runs.csv (query,run,phase,status,ms,rows,start_utc) and <out_dir>/<q>.r<i>.out (mysql --batch)
TAG=$1; DATA=$2; OUT=$3; TO=$4; RUNS=$5; shift 5
QD=/home/prestouser/aocsa/sirius-stacks-wt/perf/experimental/starrocks/benchmarks/tpch/queries
mkdir -p $OUT; echo "query,run,phase,status,ms,rows,start_utc" > $OUT/runs.csv
M="mysql --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9030 --user root --batch --connect-timeout=5"
for q in "$@"; do
  sql=$(sed "s#__TPCH_DATA__#$DATA#g" $QD/$q.sql)
  for i in $(seq 0 $RUNS); do
    phase=warm; [ $i = 0 ] && phase=cold
    start=$(date -u +%FT%T.%3N); t0=$(date +%s%N)
    if timeout $TO $M -e "/* $TAG $q r$i */ $sql" > $OUT/$q.r$i.out 2> $OUT/$q.r$i.err; then st=pass; else st=fail; rc=$?; fi
    ms=$(( ($(date +%s%N) - t0) / 1000000 )); rows=$(( $(wc -l < $OUT/$q.r$i.out) - 1 )); [ $rows -lt 0 ] && rows=0
    [ $st = fail ] && [ $ms -ge $((TO*1000 - 500)) ] && st=timeout
    echo "$q,$i,$phase,$st,$ms,$rows,$start" >> $OUT/runs.csv
    echo "$q r$i $phase $st ${ms}ms rows=$rows $( [ $st != pass ] && head -c 160 $OUT/$q.r$i.err | tr '\n' ' ')"
    [ $st != pass ] && break   # a failing run skips the rest of that query (bench.sh semantics)
  done
done

Source: TableFunctionTable.java:264 -> getFileSchema() :688 -> BackendServiceClient.getFileSchema :712 (no cache); compute_node_service.rs:683 get_file_schema handler; file_schema.rs:62-75 parquet_files_schema reads every file footer serially (60 for lineitem); Deployer.java:164-216 deployFragments: for each stage deployAsync then waitForDeploymentCompletion before the next stage; engine.rs:1-14 exec_plan_fragment returns without waiting for execution (rendezvous reorders), so the phased deploy buys nothing on this CN
findings.impact: A constant ~0.2-0.27 s per query; for q11 it is 236 ms of 969 (1 CN) and 267 of 663 (4 CN), for q02 ~200 of 1264/1154, for q22 similar. It is the dominant reason the fragment-heavy small queries sit at 1.8-2.9x of standalone and scale 1.1-1.5x on 4 CNs.
findings.proposed_change: (1) Cache FILES() schema inference: in the CN get_file_schema handler (compute_node_service.rs:683 / file_schema.rs) key on (resolved path list, mtime/size) and read the footers concurrently instead of the serial loop at file_schema.rs:62-75; or in the FE TableFunctionTable.getFileSchema keyed on the path glob + format (saves 60-110 ms/query; confidence high). (2) Deploy all fragments in one wave for the Sirius CN: Deployer.deployFragments waits stage by stage although the CN's exec_plan_fragment returns immediately and the receiver-first rendezvous (local_exchange.rs) tolerates any arrival order -- collapse threeStageExecutionsToDeploy into a single deployAsync + wait, or expose a session variable to do so (saves 40-110 ms; confidence medium). (3) Bench-kit hygiene: define only the CTEs a query uses (saves 5-6 of the 8 RPCs today; confidence high but does not fix real users).

findings.claim: Each CN executes fragments strictly one at a time on the single engine thread, so independent leaf fragments never overlap and the query span is the sum of fragment runs plus rendezvous gaps; the gaps are 6-8% of the span on 1 CN but 31% on 4 CNs (cross-CN sender barriers), and the executor's 4 slots idle during the many 1-task fragments.
evidence: Measured cn1/cluster.log q02.r1: 13 fragments start only after the previous one finished (56b 47 ms | 56a 5 | 569 5 | 56d 204 | 56c 81 | 565 5 | 568 7 | 567 4 | 566 443 | 564 113 | 563 16 | 562 41 | 561 6): sum 977 ms, span 1067 ms, gaps 90 ms; q11.r1: the two independent partsupp scan fragments a90 (35.009-35.359) and a8d (35.395-35.684) run back to back, sum 688 of span 733 ms; q15.r1: the two lineitem fragments 567 (03.370-05.624) and 566 (05.642-07.805) serial

Measured cn4/cluster.log q02.r1 cn0: 13 instances sum 748 ms, span 40.301->41.382 = 1081 ms, gaps 333 ms (31%), largest before receivers (45a->452 71 ms, 452->44e 50 ms, 44e->44b 28 ms) i.e. waiting for the other three CNs' senders + nixl transmit before the receiver can declare its stream cardinality; identical pattern on the other three CNs

Measured slot use: cn1-quent.txt q02.r1 -- 9 of 13 fragments have 1-5 tasks and Comp 1-43 ms (nation/region/supplier scans, merge and result fragments), while the whole query's Comp is 2.9 s (reservation-ratio.txt cn1 q02.r1: 133 tasks, Comp 2.9 s, Queued 0.3 s, wall 1.06 s -> 2.7 of 4 slots busy on average)

Source: engine.rs:1-14 ('the single process-global context serializes fragment execution -- both lifted by the streaming evolution'), engine.rs:278-282 `while let Ok(request) = requests.recv() { EngineRequest::Run(request) => run_fragment(...) }` one request at a time; sender outputs are parked (dwell_max 0.98 s for fragment 56b in cn1-quent.txt:104) until the receiver's turn
findings.impact: For q02/q11 on 1 CN a lower bound of total Comp / 4 slots (0.73 s and 0.5 s) versus the measured 1.07 s and 0.73 s spans, i.e. 25-35% of the engine span is serialization and gaps; on 4 CNs the rendezvous gaps alone are ~0.33 s of q02's 1.08 s, and they grow with fragment count (q02 has 49 instances on 4 CNs). Combined with MFS-3 this is why q02/q11/q22 stop scaling.
findings.proposed_change: Let the engine thread accept a new Run while earlier fragments are executing: run each fragment on its own DuckDB connection over the shared SiriusContext (the C++ executor already multiplexes tasks from several pipelines over its 4 slots) and keep only the parked-output bookkeeping on the engine thread; start with leaf (sender) fragments, whose outputs are parked anyway, so independent scans overlap and receivers no longer wait for a fully idle engine. Measure with the same cluster.log timelines: target span ~ critical path (q02 1 CN: 566->564->563->562->561 = 0.62 s). Confidence medium: engine.rs says the serialization is a known limitation 'lifted by the streaming evolution'; correctness of concurrent fragments on one context needs the C++ side checked.

findings.claim: On 4 CNs the first partsupp scan of q02 (fragment ...c472, feeding the ps_partkey shuffle) reads 3.2 GB per CN at 4.9 GB/s while the second partsupp scan in the same run (...c464) reads 3.3 GB at 20 GB/s with the same task count, making that one fragment 348 ms = 32% of the 1081 ms span on every CN; cause not established, and the scan_split_read Quent probe reports 0 bytes on this path so it cannot help.
evidence: Measured cn4-quent.json q02.r1 fragment ...c472: tasks 2, Computing 0.668 s, GPU_SCAN(0) 0.663 s for input 3.22 GB, 10 batches, dwell max 0.217 s; fragment ...c464: tasks 2, GPU_SCAN(0) 0.164 s for 3.29 GB, 12 batches; both 'scan_reads': {'n': 2, 'bytes': 0, 'ns': 0}
Measured cn4/cluster.log q02.r1: c472/473/474/475 run 40.433->40.781 (348 ms) on all four CNs; c464-467 run ~96 ms; the four c472-class fragments are the longest fragments of the query

Measured reference rates: cn1-quent.txt:103-157 fragment 56d GPU_SCAN n=5 0.788 s for 13.10 GB (16.6 GB/s per task-second) and 566 GPU_SCAN(6) 0.779 s for 13.10 GB; cn4-quent.txt q11.r1 partsupp scans 4.04-4.12 GB in 0.232-0.246 s (17 GB/s) -- so neither 'first scan of the query' nor 'partsupp on 4 CNs' is slow in general

Both fragments carry the same three partsupp columns (FE q02 plan fragments F01 and F12 project ps_partkey, ps_suppkey, ps_supplycost); the c472 output is 6.4 GB of batches vs 9.8 GB for c464 (cn4-quent.json batch_GB)

findings.proposed_change: Instrument before fixing: populate the scan_split_read probe (bytes, ns, source tier) for the parquet path used by FILES() scans, then compare c472 vs c464 in one 4-CN q02 run; candidates to check are host page-cache vs cold NVMe reads for the split assignment the FE gives the first fragment, and the per-task decoded-bytes budget (approximate_batch_size) producing 10 vs 12 batches. Confidence low on the cause; the measurement gap itself is high confidence.

findings.claim: With every FILES() scan at cardinality 1, the 4-CN q11 plan PARTITIONs the 10M-row supplier table on s_nationkey (25 distinct keys) to meet the single GERMANY nation row, producing a skewed shuffle where three of four CNs receive supplier rows that match nothing, and the engine over-reserves the partsupp join fragments 54-68x (236 GB requested for a 4.3 GB peak); both are measurable but cost little at this pool size.
evidence: Measured cn4-cnlog.txt q11.r0-r2: declared stream 2 (nation) = 0/0/1/0 rows per CN, stream 4 (supplier) = 2,398,857 / 1,200,355 / 3,201,347 / 3,199,441 rows per CN; card-compare-cn4.txt:45-54 exch 4 SHUFFLE 10,000,000 -> join 5 PARTITIONED, exch 7 BROADCAST 1,599,792 (= 4 x 399,948 German suppliers), repeated for the HAVING subquery (exch 15/17/20); cn4-transmits.txt q11 75 transmits 0.40 GB

Measured 1-CN plan for the same joins: card-compare-cn1.txt:66-67 join 4/7 BROADCAST with nation 10,000,000?? no -- exch 3 BROADCAST 10,000,000 supplier rows as the build of join 4 against nation (supplier is the broadcast/build side, nation the probe), i.e. the FE picks the big side as build in both plans

Measured reservation: reservation-ratio.txt cn1 q11.r1 req 236.2 GB vs peak 4.3 GB (54.4x), cn4 q11.r1 378.9 vs 5.6 GB (67.7x), standalone 128.8 vs 32.8 GB (3.9x); cn1-quent.txt:699-741 fragment a90 req 116.4 GB alloc 2.3 GB Rsv 0.117 s, a8d req 113.2 GB alloc 0.9 GB Rsv 0.142 s (the join output is estimated from the 800M-row parquet scan estimate against the exact 399,948-row stream)
Measured wall: the affected q11 fragments run ~20 ms each (cn4-quent.txt q11.r1 fragments ...54bb-...54c3), so the skew is not on the critical path today
findings.impact: Small today (q11 4-CN 664 ms is dominated by MFS-3's 267 ms and the two partsupp scans); the 54-68x over-reservation would start serializing tasks at pools smaller than ~1/10 of the current 100 GiB, and the skewed PARTITIONED join pattern (large table shuffled on a low-cardinality key to meet a filtered 1-row dimension) recurs in q02 exch 26/31 and would be the next bottleneck once MFS-2/3/4 are fixed.
findings.proposed_change: Same root fix as MFS-2 (row counts and NDV-less min/max for FILES() scans so nation/region/supplier are broadcast and never the shuffled side). For the reservation, use the declared exact stream cardinality (stream_bind_catalog.hpp:44-46) to bound the hash-join output estimate when the build side is an exact-cardinality stream and the probe is a parquet scan: output <= probe_rows * (build_rows / build_key_ndv) with ndv taken as build_rows for a key column, instead of the current ~probe-row-count estimate; confidence medium.
